answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example ARM id: /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/<accountName>).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name mydocdb --resource-group myrg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session. (az cosmosdb is part of the core az CLI, not a separate extension.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example Bicep: resource docdb 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'mydocdb' location: resourceGroup().location properties: { databaseAccountOfferType: 'Standard' kind: 'MongoDB' } }). Terraform (azurerm): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "mydocdb" resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-style connection string for the Azure DocumentDB (MongoDB API) endpoint: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&readPreference=primaryPreferred. Notes: scheme mongodb:// (or mongodb+srv:// if DNS SRV supported), host typically <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, TLS required (ssl=true), commonly uses port 10255 for TLS, include replicaSet=globaldb and often retryWrites=false for Cosmos compatibility.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Primary billing model is Cosmos-style throughput (Request Units per second, RU/s) — provisioned RUs or autoscale; Cosmos DB also offers a serverless option for on-demand usage. Some newer MongoDB-compatible dedicated clusters/offers may expose vCore-based SKUs (instance sizes like Mxx) for dedicated compute; however the canonical model for Cosmos (DocumentDB) is RU-based throughput or serverless. (If you need vCore-style SKUs use the dedicated MongoDB-managed offering if available in your subscription.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane authentication: standard MongoDB username/password (SCRAM—use the account's Mongo user and password or the primary key mapped to a Mongo user). Management-plane uses Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) for RBAC. For data-plane Azure AD auth: newer previews add support for Azure AD token-based auth, but the common production method is SCRAM (username/password). If using Azure AD to authenticate with the driver you would acquire an AAD access token (MSAL) and supply it via the driver auth mechanism supported by the service (e.g., SASL/OAUTHBEARER or a connection string parameter) — exact connection string parameter and authMechanism depend on the preview feature.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (Node.js: mongodb driver, or Mongoose on top of that). There's no separate service-specific Node.js SDK for MongoDB data-plane operations; Azure provides management SDKs (azurerm/azure SDKs) for provisioning and management, but application code should use the MongoDB driver/Mongoose. Example install: npm install mongoose (or npm i mongodb).

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: I believe the service exposes vector index algorithms such as DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. A speculative create-index command (Mongo-style) might look like: db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }) — but the actual syntax is provider-specific (may be created via the Azure portal/CLI/MCP server or an admin command) rather than exact Mongo createIndex options above.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text or hybrid (text+vector) search is typically done by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search): push or index Cosmos/Mongo data into an Azure Cognitive Search index (which can support text analyzers and, where available, vector search). Some Mongo-compatible offerings also include built-in vector+text search features, but the default Azure pattern is to use Azure Cognitive Search for advanced text/hybrid search.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: The MongoDB wire protocol version supported depends on the account API version; historically Cosmos DB Mongo API supported earlier MongoDB server versions (3.x, 4.0, 4.2) and newer accounts add support for later wire protocol versions (5.x/6.x); the sample environment mentions MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol which implies support up to 7.0 in that deployment. Commonly-missing features historically include some server-side JS ($where), certain aggregation stages or filesystem-level features, and occasional differences in transaction semantics; always test features such as multi-document transactions, change streams, and $lookup at your target API version.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Windows) but it historically supports the SQL API best and is limited for MongoDB API. For reliable local development run a local MongoDB server image instead: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:6.0 and use mongodb://localhost:27017. For TLS-testing against Cosmos features you must test against the real Azure endpoint (commonly port 10255) since the emulator may not fully emulate Mongo features.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are supported on MongoDB API accounts that expose a replica-set-like behavior and on supported wire-protocol versions; you consume them via the driver (collection.watch() / db.watch()). Ensure your account supports the MongoDB server version that includes change streams (4.0+ or later) and that the account is configured to allow them — in many cases nothing else must be enabled other than using the correct API version, but some accounts or SKUs may require a feature flag/preview to enable change streams.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The service-specific MCP server is named documentdb (use the 'documentdb' MCP server). The general Azure MCP Server provides management tooling for many services, but for data-plane inspection and Mongo-specific index/plan tooling you should use the documentdb MCP server/connection profile that targets the cluster. (I expect the general Azure MCP Server covers management but the documentdb MCP server supplies Mongo/DocumentDB-specific data-plane tools.)

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft used the name DocumentDB for the original Azure document database offering; that service evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. "Azure DocumentDB" is therefore lineage of Cosmos DB; the Azure Cosmos DB MongoDB API implements the Mongo wire protocol on top of Cosmos DB's engine. This is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB; Cosmos/DocumentDB is Microsoft-managed proprietary engine with multiple API frontends (SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Microsoft’s Cosmos DB proprietary engine that emulates the MongoDB wire protocol for the Mongo API. Application code should use the standard MongoDB drivers but be aware of subtle semantics differences (consistency, RU/throughput behaviour, some unsupported server-side features) and that certain admin/ops features may be different. Transaction and indexing behavior and performance characteristics can differ from a vanilla MongoDB server.

answers.question: What connection settings will the Node.js Mongoose sample use and where are they read from?
answers.answer: The sample will read the Mongo connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and connect with Mongoose using options { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000 }. Example connect call: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true });

answers.question: What transaction/session options will the sample use to do the multi-document decrement+insert atomically?
answers.answer: Use MongoDB sessions and transactions from the driver: const session = await mongoose.startSession(); session.startTransaction({ readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' }, writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } }); perform updates/inserts with { session } and commitTransaction()/abortTransaction().

answers.question: How will optimistic locking be implemented in the sample?
answers.answer: Use a numeric version field (e.g. __v or version). When updating a document use a conditional update that checks the version: db.inventory.updateOne({ _id: id, version: currentVersion }, { $inc: { quantity: -1 }, $set: { version: currentVersion + 1 } }, { session }). If matchedCount is 0 treat as a version conflict and surface a clear error to the caller.

answers.question: What failure cases will the sample explicitly handle and how will they be surfaced?
answers.answer: Handle (1) Out-of-stock: detect stock <= 0 before decrement or detect matchedCount==0 after conditional decrement and return a clear 409/OutOfStock error. (2) Optimistic lock failure: return 409/Conflict with message 'version conflict'. (3) Transaction aborts/retryable errors: retry the transaction up to N times (e.g., 3) on transient errors, otherwise return 500 with details. All errors return JSON with code, message and a small detail field for debugging.

answers.question: What indexes and collection setup will the sample create before running?
answers.answer: Create two collections in database sample_retail_05: carts and inventory. For inventory: ensure unique index on sku (_id or sku), and an index on version (if used) and any fields queried. For carts: index on userId. Example operations run at startup: db.createCollection('inventory'); db.inventory.createIndex({ sku: 1 }, { unique: true }); db.createCollection('carts'); db.carts.createIndex({ userId: 1 });
